title: 8.1 Decision Making Under Uncertainty
bodyHtml:
8.1 Decision Making Under Uncertainty

Why This Matters

Many people grow up thinking:

good decision = good result

That works in some parts of life.

Trading is harder.

In markets, you can:

  • follow the rules;
  • size the trade correctly;
  • wait for a solid setup;
  • still lose on that one trade.

That does not automatically mean the decision was bad.

If beginners do not understand this, they often become unstable very quickly:

  • one loss makes them abandon a good process;
  • one win makes them trust a bad process.

Both reactions are dangerous.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain why a good process can still produce a loss;
  • separate process quality from single-trade outcome quality;
  • name what a trader can control and what a trader cannot control.

Process and Outcome Are Not the Same Thing

A process is the method you used:

  • your setup rules;
  • your position size;
  • your entry and exit plan;
  • your discipline.

An outcome is what happened after the trade:

  • win;
  • loss;
  • small gain;
  • stopped out;
  • target reached.

In uncertain markets, those two things do not always match in the short term.

A Simple Process-Outcome Table

Situation What happened What the trader should learn
Good process, good outcome Rules were followed and the trade won Keep the discipline and still review calmly
Good process, bad outcome Rules were followed and the trade lost Accept that losses are part of uncertain markets
Bad process, good outcome Rules were broken and the trade still won Do not let luck train bad habits
Bad process, bad outcome Rules were broken and the trade lost Fix the process before thinking about money again

(Table alt-text: A four-row table showing how good or bad process can combine with winning or losing outcomes, plus the lesson each situation should teach.)

This table is not theory for one market only.

It can describe:

  • a careful EUR/USD trade that still loses after a surprise dollar move;
  • a disciplined Nasdaq trade that still fails after a rate shock;
  • a well-planned gold trade that loses when the market focus changes;
  • a bad Brent crude trade that wins once because of luck.

Good Process and Bad Outcome

Imagine this trade:

  • the trend is clear;
  • the entry follows your checklist;
  • the stop is placed where the plan says it should be;
  • the size fits your risk rule.

Then unexpected news hits the market and your stop is triggered.

The trade lost. But the process may still have been good.

That matters because beginners often make the wrong conclusion:

I lost, so my whole method must be broken

That is not always true.

Sometimes the market simply delivered one losing result inside a larger uncertain process.

Bad Process and Good Outcome

This is the more dangerous trap.

Imagine a trader:

  • ignores the checklist;
  • enters from boredom;
  • risks too much;
  • wins anyway.

The account balance went up. But the process was weak.

If the trader learns the wrong lesson from that win, the next bad decision may cost much more.

Luck can hide bad habits.

What You Can Control

You cannot control:

  • the next headline;
  • the next candle;
  • what other traders do;
  • whether one trade wins or loses.

You can control:

  • whether the setup matches your rules;
  • how much you risk;
  • whether you follow the plan;
  • whether you review the trade honestly.

That is why good traders focus on process first.

One Simple Example

Suppose your plan says:

  • risk 1%;
  • buy only after a pullback;
  • place the stop below a clear structure point.

You follow the plan exactly on a trade in EUR/USD, a stock-index product, gold, or Brent crude. The trade still loses.

The right review question is not:

why did the market betray me?

The better question is:

did I follow a sound process?

If the answer is yes, the loss may be normal.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Treating Every Loss as Proof of Failure

One loss does not automatically mean the idea or method is useless.

Mistake 2: Treating Every Win as Proof of Skill

Short-term wins can come from luck, poor discipline, or both.

Mistake 3: Trying to Control the Uncontrollable

Risk management controls exposure. It does not force the market to reward you immediately.

Mistake 4: Reviewing Emotion Before Reviewing Process

Feelings matter, but the first question should still be:

did I follow the plan?

quizItems.prompt: What is the main lesson about uncertainty in trading?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A good process can still lead to a losing trade

choices.label: B
choices.text: A good process guarantees a win

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every losing trade proves the setup was bad

correctAnswer.label: A
correctAnswer.text: A good process can still lead to a losing trade

quizItems.explanation: The lesson teaches that outcome and decision quality are not identical in uncertain markets.

quizItems.prompt: Which item is mostly under the trader's control?
quizItems.explanation: The lesson separates controllable actions such as size and execution from uncontrollable market results.

quizItems.prompt: After a difficult trade, what should be reviewed first?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether luck should be blamed only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether size should be doubled next time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether the journal should be ignored

quizItems.explanation: The lesson teaches process-first review instead of outcome-first self-judgment.
